inline.s: The Distinct Preface: The common preface is followed by the distinct preface, which is the part of the introduction that differs from chapter to chapter. For example, the second passage of this sūtra (“At that time, the World-Honored One, during the meal hour, donned his robe and took up his bowl, entered the great city of Shravasti to beg for alms. Within that city, having begged in succession, he returned to his dwelling. When the meal was finished, he put away his robe and bowl, washed his feet, and arranged his seat to sit.”) is the distinct preface. The distinct preface is also called the “introductory preface” (fāqǐ xù), because it explains how this Dharma assembly was initiated.

The Main Body (zhèngzōng fēn) is the part where this sūtra sets forth its proper teaching. Of the sūtra's thirty-two divisions, the Main Body runs from the second division to the end of the thirty-first.

The Circulating Division (liútōng fēn) lists the benefits of upholding this sūtra, exhorting beings to uphold it, recite it, study it, and circulate it. In this sūtra, the final division (the thirty-second, “Embodying Transformations Are Not Real”) is the Circulating Division.

blocks.text: Division One: The Occasion of the Dharma Assembly

inline.s: The Occasion of the Dharma Assembly” (fǎhuì yīnyóu) means the cause and origin of this sūtra, that is, of the Vajra (Diamond) Dharma assembly. The character “division” (fēn) is equivalent to “chapter” (zhāng). For example, “The Occasion of the Dharma Assembly, Division One” means “Chapter One: The Occasion of the Dharma Assembly.”

This division (“The Occasion of the Dharma Assembly, Division One”) is the Introduction (xù fēn). The Introduction is the part that recounts the causes by which this sūtra was initiated. As mentioned before, the Introduction is further divided into two parts: the common preface and the distinct preface.

Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was staying in the Jetavana Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in the kingdom of Shravasti, together with a large assembly of great bhikshus, twelve hundred and fifty of them.
This is what I personally saw and heard. At that time the Buddha was at the Jetavana Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in Shravasti, together with twelve hundred and fifty great bhikshus.

【Thus have I heard】This is what I personally saw and heard. “Thus have I heard” is a guarantee of trustworthiness, proving that this sūtra was indeed spoken by the Buddha and that the recorded text is correct and without error. When the Buddha was about to enter nirvāṇa, he instructed the Venerable Ānanda: when the scriptures are gathered together in the future, place the phrase “Thus have I heard” at the head of every sūtra, to certify that it was indeed spoken by the Buddha and to distinguish it from the scriptures of non-Buddhists. 【At one time】At that time. This denotes the time when the Buddha spoke this sūtra—that is, when teacher and disciples were in accord, and when the faculties of beings met the teaching. The Tathāgata's teaching extends across humans and gods, and its transmission is spread throughout the world; because the years, months, and days of each recounting could never be identical, the phrase “at one time” is used to record it. 【Teacher and student】Teacher and student; master and disciple. 【The faculties meet the teaching】“Faculties” (jī) is the capacity of the audience; “teaching” (jiào) is the Buddha's instruction. The faculties of beings differ, so the Buddha teaches each according to its capacity, giving deep or shallow teaching to match. “The faculties meet the teaching” means that the spiritual faculties of the assembly and the Buddha's teaching are in harmonious correspondence. 【Buddha】An abbreviation of “Buddha,” here referring to Shakyamuni Buddha. “Buddha” is the Sanskrit sound, rendered in Chinese as “the Awakened One.” Inwardly one awakens, free of all deluded thoughts; outwardly one awakens, no longer defiled by the six sense objects.

【Shravasti】Its location is in the northwestern part of present-day India, on the southern bank of the Rapti River; the king at that time was Prasenajit. 【Jetavana Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada's Park】A park in the capital of Shravasti where Shakyamuni Buddha taught this sūtra. The trees of this park belonged to Prince Jeta of Shravasti, while the land belonged to the elder Anāthapiṇḍada; together the two offered them to the Buddha, hence the name “Jetavana Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada's Park,” meaning the grove of Prince Jeta and the park of the elder Anāthapiṇḍada. The Buddha often taught the Dharma there. 【Great bhikshu】“Bhikshu” is the general term for one who has left home and received the full precepts; men are called “bhikshu” and women “bhikshunī.” “Great bhikshu” refers to a bhikshu of lofty virtue and advanced years. 【Together】Together.

At that time, the World-Honored One, during the meal hour, donned his robe and took up his bowl, entered the great city of Shravasti to beg for alms. Within that city, having begged in succession from door to door, he returned to his own place. When the meal was finished, he put away his robe and bowl, washed his feet, arranged his seat, and sat down.

At this time, the hour of the single midday meal had arrived, so the World-Honored One put on his great robe and took up his alms bowl, and leading his disciples, with solemn, dignified deportment and unhurried steps, entered the capital of Shravasti to beg for alms. In that city without distinguishing between the poor and humble and the wealthy and noble, he begged in order from house to house with his bowl. When his alms-seeking was done, he returned to his dwelling. After the World-Honored One finished his meal, he put away his robe and bowl, washed his feet, and arranged his seat; with serene dignity he sat cross-legged, his right mindfulness motionless.
Yuan-Wei

The translation by Bodhiruci says: “At that time, the World-Honored One, during the meal hour, donned his robe and took up his bowl, entered the great city of Shravasti to beg for alms. Within that city, having begged for alms in due order, he returned to his own place. When the meal was finished, he put away his robe and bowl, washed his feet, and as usual arranged his seat and sat cross-legged. His body upright, he dwelt with right mindfulness motionless.”

This passage is the distinct preface. The distinct preface is the part that differs from sūtra to sūtra within the Introduction, and it comes after the common preface. The distinct preface is also called the “introductory preface,” because it explains how the Dharma assembly of this sūtra was initiated.

The initiation of this sūtra's Dharma assembly is the World-Honored One's showing, through his everyday activities (donning the robe, taking up the bowl, entering the city to beg alms, even arranging the seat and sitting), that prajñā is everywhere present—teaching by personal example what awakening is and what the original scenery of one's own nature is.

【At that time】At that time. 【World-Honored One】A reverent title of the Buddha. Because the Buddha, endowed with all virtues, is revered by the world and stands uniquely supreme in the world, he is called the World-Honored One. 【Meal hour】The hour of the single midday meal had arrived. In the Sūtra of the Forty-Two Sections, the Buddha said: “Shave off your hair and beard and become a shramana; one who receives the Dharma, having abandoned worldly wealth, seeks only as much as is enough by begging. Eat one meal at midday, sleep one night under a tree—beware of doing more! What deludes people is love and desire.”

【Donning the robe】The three robes and one bowl are the personal possessions of a bhikshu. The three robes are the antarvāsaka, the uttarāsaṅga, and the saṃghāṭī; these three robes are all called kaṣāya in Sanskrit (“kaṣāya” originally means “dyed, impure-colored robe,” because the dharma robe worn by one who has left home must all be dyed a muddy, defiled color). The antarvāsaka is rendered in Chinese as the “body robe,” made of five strips (that is, five squares of cloth sewn together in a field-like pattern, hence the name “field-merit robe”); it is worn for work and for sitting and lying down. The uttarāsaṅga is worn over the antarvāsaka, hence its name “upper robe,” made of seven strips; it is worn when performing ceremonies and entering the assembly. The saṃghāṭī is rendered as the “robe of gathering together,” also called the “great robe,” made of from nine to twenty-five strips; it is worn on solemn occasions. Now, about to enter the city to beg for alms, the Buddha therefore specially wore the great robe.

【Bowl】The alms bowl, an abbreviation of the Sanskrit pattra; it is the bhikshu's vessel for food. 【Great city of Shravasti】The capital of Shravasti; the Jetavana Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada's Park lay five or six li to the southeast of the city. 【Beg for alms】A bhikshu, free from all greed and craving and subduing his pride, constantly goes begging for alms to sustain this physical body and to aid the accomplishment of the path. 【Beg in succession】When a bhikshu begs for alms, he is not attached to flavors, does not slight beings, does not choose between rich and poor, but with a mind of equanimity seeks alms house by house in due order; he may not go beyond seven houses or beyond the appointed time, and even if his bowl is not filled, he must return. 【His own place】The place of his dwelling, the Jetavana Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada's Park. 【Finished】Finished.

When the Buddha taught other sūtras, he often initiated them by emitting light and manifesting auspicious signs. This sūtra, however, is the mind-dharma of the Tathāgata's Buddhahood, yet it is initiated by everyday activities—this truly has deep significance. It shows that prajñā is nowhere else than in daily activities. The Platform Sūtra of the Sixth Patriarch says: “Ordinary beings are the Buddha; afflictions are bodhi. If the previous thought is deluded, one is an ordinary being; if the later thought is awakened, one is a Buddha. If the previous thought is attached to objects, one is in affliction; if the later thought is free of objects, one is in bodhi.” This sūtra says: “Depart from all marks, and that is called all Buddhas.” The World-Honored One's manifestation is thought after thought of awakening, thought after thought free of objects—in donning the robe, taking up the bowl, entering the city to beg, even in arranging the seat and sitting, he everywhere reveals the wondrous import of prajñā—“not grasping at marks, ever still and unmoved”—in order to proclaim the Vajra Prajñāpāramitā, so that the great assembly may all learn and realize in daily life what the original scenery of one's own nature is.

【Not grasping at marks, ever still and unmoved】Not grasping at marks as true, and therefore not being moved by them. That is, not to be attached to marks, not to move the mind. 【Original scenery】Also called “the original face,” it is a phrase used in the Chan lineage to describe the original state of one's own nature (the state of complete awakening).

There is a story like this. A woman went to ask the Buddha: “How can I attain enlightenment?” The Buddha said: “What is your work?” She said: “I make my living by drawing water.” The Buddha told her: “When you draw water, be clearly and distinctly aware of every movement in your mind (do not let unconscious habitual movements appear).” The woman earnestly practiced according to the Buddha's teaching and attained enlightenment.

Be clearly aware of every movement”—this is the wondrous method of mindfully illuminating the present moment and bringing practice into everyday life. If one can do this, one will no longer worry about having no time to practice, and will never again be restless and anxious, fearing that one is missing out on practice. How can one make practice part of daily life? Never lose mindful illumination! At all times and in all places, never lose mindful illumination; be clearly aware of one's own mind and actions, and not be turned by circumstances.

The Buddha is awakening itself. The Buddha is an awakened one who has already woken from the dream of ignorance. Though his daily life is the same as that of ordinary people, his realm is completely different—at every moment it is awareness that radiates light.

The World-Honored One manifested how to practice in daily life: when conditions arise, respond; when conditions cease, become still. In responding he never lost mindful illumination, ever serene and free—as the saying goes, “not grasping at marks, ever still and unmoved.”

In just this way, through the everyday activities of donning the robe, taking up the bowl, begging for alms, returning to his dwelling, eating the meal, putting away the robe and bowl, washing his feet, arranging his seat and sitting, the World-Honored One teaches us that we can practice at no time and in no place, and points out for us people toiling in the dust a convenient means of entry. Hence in the following text the elder Subhuti exclaims in wonder and says: The Tathāgata acts thus—this is truly perfect protection and care for all bodhisattvas, and a perfect entrusting and instruction of all bodhisattvas!

Practice is of two kinds: practice on the seat and practice off the seat. Practice on the seat is drill; practice off the seat is actual combat. If used well, there is no time and no place that is not practice. The Sixth Patriarch says: “What is called sitting meditation? In this Dharma-gate, without obstruction, without hindrance (unrestrained by conditions and objects). Outwardly, toward all wholesome and unwholesome states, the thought does not arise—this is called sitting; inwardly, seeing one's own nature unmoving—this is called meditation.” The verse says: “A day of practice is a day of merit; a day without practice is a day empty; true practice lies in everyday life—the Way of the Buddha in daily living itself.”

There was a practitioner named Bāhiya who, having traveled a long distance and covered with dust, hurried to Shravasti to seek the Dharma from the Buddha. Just then he saw the Buddha going from house to house begging for alms with his bowl, every gesture elegant and beautiful, his six sense faculties fully tamed and guarded, serene and still. Bāhiya approached and bowed, asking the Buddha to teach him the Dharma, to teach him the Dharma of immeasurable benefit and peace. The Buddha said that at that moment, while going from door to door with his bowl, it was not suitable to teach. But Bāhiya asked repeatedly, so the Buddha taught him there on the spot: “Bāhiya! You should train yourself thus: in the seen there will be only the seen; in the heard, only the heard; in the cognized, only the cognized; in the discerned, only the discerned. Bāhiya! When you can train yourself so that in the seen there is only the seen... then you will have no clinging and no obstruction. If you have no clinging and no obstruction, then you will not be in this world nor in the next. Not being in these two worlds, all sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress will wholly be dissolved.” (The original text is found in the tenth section of the first chapter of the Udāna in the Theravāda canon.)

【The three times】The past, the present, and the future. What has already arisen and already ceased is called “the past world”; what has arisen but not yet ceased is called “the present world”; what has not yet arisen or appeared is called “the future world.”

Note: “If you have no clinging and no obstruction, then you will not be in this world nor in the next. Not being in these two worlds, all sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress will wholly be dissolved.” It seems it should read: “If you have no clinging and no obstruction, then you will not be in the past world nor in the future world. Not being in these two worlds, all sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress will wholly be dissolved.” This may be a transcription error.

blocks.text: Division Two: Subhuti Rises and Requests

inline.s: Subhuti (shànxiàn)” is the Chinese rendering of Subhuti's name. Subhuti rises from his seat and beseeches the World-Honored One to teach the Dharma. From this division onward, this sūtra enters the Main Body.

At that time, the elder Subhuti, in the midst of the great assembly, then rose from his seat, uncovered his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence addressed the Buddha, saying: How rare, O World-Honored One! The Tathāgata protects and cares for all bodhisattvas and perfectly entrusts and instructs all bodhisattvas. World-Honored One! Good men and good women who have awakened the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—how should they abide? How should they subdue their minds?

At this time, the elder Subhuti, in the midst of the assembly, then rose from his seat. Uncovering his right shoulder, kneeling his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, he said to the Buddha: How supremely excellent, O World-Honored One! Setting your very body as the standard, you thus teach by example in every time and place—this is truly the best protection and care for all bodhisattvas and the best education and guidance for all bodhisattvas! World-Honored One! Good men and good women who have aroused the great mind to become a Buddha and to save beings—how should they abide? How should they subdue their minds?

How should they abide? How should they subdue their minds?”—this is the main theme of this sūtra. The first part of this sūtra answers these two questions; at the very beginning of its latter part (Division Seventeen, “The Ultimate Purity of the Non-Self”), Subhuti again raises these two questions, and the World-Honored One answers them still more fully.
For whom is the Diamond Sūtra spoken? From this passage we can know: the Buddha spoke this sūtra for ordinary beings who have aroused the great mind.

【At that time】At this time, that is, when the World-Honored One had finished sitting in stillness. 【Elder】An elder bhikshu of advanced age and lofty virtue. 【Subhuti】One of the Buddha's ten great disciples; in Chinese rendered as Kōngshēng (“only-empty”), Shànxiàn (“good manifestation”), and Shànjí (“good fortune”); among the ten great disciples he is renowned as “foremost in comprehending emptiness.” 【Uncovering the right shoulder】When wearing the kaṣāya, the right shoulder is uncovered and the left shoulder covered. This was originally an ancient Indian gesture of respect; Buddhism adopted it, so that when a bhikshu pays respects to the Buddha or greets his teacher, the right shoulder must be bared, signifying readiness for service and for being commanded. 【Stating】To state one's case from below to the superior. 【How rare】How supremely excellent! An exclamation of praise. 【Tathāgata】One of the Buddha's ten epithets. Generally, “World-Honored One” is the general title used in address; “Buddha” denotes the fruit of virtue; “Tathāgata” denotes the virtue of the true nature.
【The Ten Epithets of the Buddha】

The Buddha has ten reverent titles: First, Tathāgata—the Buddha comes riding the path of true reality, arrives at perfect enlightenment, and manifests across the three realms. Second, Arhat (Worthy of Offerings)—the Buddha is worthy of offerings from humans and gods. Third, Samyaksaṃbuddha (Perfectly Enlightened)—the Buddha truly and perfectly knows all dharmas. Fourth, Illuminate of Conduct and Wisdom Purified—the Buddha is fully possessed of the three insights (the insight into past lives, the insight into the heavenly eye, the insight into the extinction of defilements) and the five practices (the holy practice, the pure practice, the heavenly practice, the infant practice, and the sick practice). Fifth, Sugata (Well-Gone)—the Buddha, free and at ease, well gone into nirvāṇa. Sixth, Lokavid (Knower of the World)—the Buddha can understand all worldly matters and principles. Seventh, Anuttara (Unsurpassed)—the Buddha is the most exalted being. Eighth, Puruṣa-damya-sārathi (Tamer of Men)—the Buddha is the great man who tames and governs all beings, leading them free from defilement into nirvāṇa. Ninth, Śāsta deva-manuṣyāṇām (Teacher of Gods and Humans)—the Buddha is the teacher of all gods and humans. Tenth, Bhagavān (World-Honored One)—the Buddha is the one revered by all beings in the world.

【The Tathāgata protects and cares for all bodhisattvas and perfectly entrusts and instructs all bodhisattvas.】“Protect and care” (hùniàn) means to protect and nurture with compassion. “Entrust and instruct” (fùzhǔ) means to entrust and enjoin, which carries the sense of teaching as well. This sentence is Subhuti's supreme praise of the World-Honored One who, setting his own body as the standard, protects, nurtures, and instructs all bodhisattvas in every time and place. 【Good men and good women】Good men and good women who observe the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions. 【Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi】Perfect, supreme wisdom—the wisdom of the Buddha. In Chinese rendered as “supreme, right, perfect enlightenment” (wúshàng zhèngděng zhèngjué), also called “supreme right, universal knowledge.” 【To awaken the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi】To arouse the great mind toward Buddhahood. “Awakening the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi” is also abbreviated as “awakening the bodhi mind.” Nāgārjuna Bodhisattva's Great Perfection of Wisdom Treatise

Forty-One” says: “When the bodhisattva first awakens the mind, taking as its basis the unsurpassed Way, thinking ‘I shall become a Buddha’—this is called the bodhi mind.” 【How】This word (yúnhé) has several meanings: why, for what reason; how, what should be done, in what manner. 【How should they abide?】“How should they abide?” (yúnhé yīng zhù) is by construction “Should they abide how?” (yīng yúnhé zhù); this uses inversion, placing “should” after the question word so as to strengthen the tone. (The answer to “How should they abide?” is in Division Four: “Give with non-attachment to marks.” Non-attachment to marks is emptiness; giving is compassion; compassion and emptiness working together—this is the bodhisattva way.) 【How should they subdue their minds?】How should they subdue their minds? (The answer is in Division Three: with a single mind to save all beings entirely, yet without the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a being, and the mark of a life. This is the wondrous means of countering affliction. As the saying goes: to stop boiling water by skimming it is not as good as drawing away the firewood from beneath the pot. With a single mind to save all beings entirely and to be free of the four marks—this too is compassion and emptiness working together.) 【Inversion】Inversion, a rhetorical device that reverses word order to strengthen the tone, to coordinate rhythm, or to vary the syntax; it is frequently used in classical Chinese, so one should be alert to it when reading the Buddhist scriptures.

The World-Honored One daily manifests in this way (not grasping at marks, ever still and unmoved), yet the great assembly does not awaken to it. Only today was the thread discerned by Subhuti, foremost in comprehending emptiness, who saw the Tathāgata's whole painstaking intent and praised it endlessly. When the World-Honored One sat in stillness, Subhuti immediately rose from his seat, uncovered his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence addressed the Buddha: How supremely excellent, O World-Honored One! Setting your very body as the standard, not grasping at marks and ever still and unmoved, you thus teach by example in every time and place—this is truly the best protection and care for all bodhisattvas and the best education and guidance for all bodhisattvas!

But why is it that the bodhisattvas cannot attain “not grasping at marks, ever still and unmoved”? For this reason Subhuti asked the World-Honored One: how should they abide, and how should they subdue their minds?

In accord with the Buddha's fundamental vow, he wished only to set forth the truth completely (to lay bare the truth of life and the universe in its entirety) so that every person may become a Buddha. But beings are thin in virtue and heavy in defilement, with timid and weak hearts, unable to bear the burden, so that it is difficult to speak plainly. (As this sūtra's Division Fourteen says: “If again there be a person who, hearing this sūtra, is not frightened, not terrified, not alarmed—one should know that this person is supremely rare.” Again, at the assembly of the Lotus Sūtra, Śāriputra three times begged the World-Honored One to reveal the first, most rare, and hard-to-understand Dharma; when the World-Honored One began to expound it, five thousand bhikshus refused to listen and withdrew from the assembly.) Therefore the Buddha had to resort to skillful, convenient means and to accommodate them, and so it is called “good” (shàn).

The World-Honored One, manifesting thus day after day, truly gives all bodhisattvas the most skillful protection and care and the most skillful entrusting and instruction. As the saying goes: rather than teaching by words, he turns them by his very body—the painstaking heart of a skilled craftsman.

In this division's passage, the phrase “How should they abide?” (yúnhé yīng zhù) has two readings. The Qianlong Canon and the standard text adopt “yúnhé yīng zhù?”, while another reading, advanced on the basis of Tang-dynasty manuscripts and Ming-dynasty printings, holds that the sentence should be “yīng yúnhé zhù?” Which is correct—“yúnhé yīng zhù” or “yīng yúnhé zhù”? This book follows the Qianlong Canon and the standard text and adopts “yúnhé yīng zhù?”

The reason is: the meaning of “How should they abide?” (yúnhé yīng zhù) is in fact “Should they abide how?” (yīng yúnhé zhù)—only that, in order to strengthen the tone, an inverted construction is used, placing “should” after the question word. Inversion is extremely common in rhetoric, used to strengthen the tone and to make the wording vivid. For example, in the Liezi

“The Foolish Old Man Removes the Mountains,” the line “How unwise you are indeed!” means: your lack of wisdom is great indeed! In Wei Zheng's “Expressing My Feelings,” “Ancient trees resound with the cold birds; the empty mountains echo with the night apes” means: in the ancient trees the cold birds sing; on the empty mountains the night apes cry. In fact, the four characters “Thus have I heard” at the very start of the sūtra are also an inversion. If translated as “I heard thus,” not only would the force of the wording and the elegance of the style be greatly weakened, but the artistic conception would differ by heaven and earth as well.
Question: Why is “How should they abide?” interpreted as “How should they sustain their dwelling?”

Answer: The phrase “How should they abide?” as translated by Master Kumārajīva is rendered extremely well; this word “abide” (zhù) fits the passages before and after it perfectly, thread by thread. (For example, the last sentence of Division Four: “Subhuti! A bodhisattva should thus abide as taught.”) But the meaning of “abide” here must be explained correctly. What a practitioner cares about most is three questions: how to dwell the mind (to gather in the mind so that it is not scattered), how to practice (to correct the actual conduct of one's body, speech, and mind), and how to subdue the mind. Judging from the other translations, in the original Sanskrit Subhuti raised these three questions. For example, Master Xuanzang's translation: “World-Honored One! Those who are intent on the bodhisattva vehicle—how should they abide? How should they practice? How should they subdue their minds?” Hence some eminent teachers have criticized Master Kumārajīva's translation as “lacking one of the three questions.”

In fact, merging the two questions into one (combining “how to dwell the mind” and “how to practice” into “How should they abide?”) is also Master Kumārajīva's painstaking effort. The World-Honored One, in “Division Four: The Unhindered Practice of Non-dwelling,” answered the first two questions in a single place (How should one dwell the mind? How should one practice?) Then, in Division Ten, he explains still more fully the question of how to dwell the mind and how to practice: “Mahāsattva bodhisattvas should thus bring forth a pure mind: they should not give rise to a mind dwelling in forms, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sounds, scents, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas; they should give rise to a mind dwelling nowhere.” Therefore the master merged these two questions into one—“How should they abide?”—so that the wording reflects and echoes before and after, is succinct and pleasant on the tongue; and from the surrounding passages the reader will not find it difficult to realize that this “abide” contains both the meaning of dwelling the mind and of practicing, that is: how to sustain one's dwelling.

After Master Kumārajīva first translated the Diamond Sūtra, another five translations successively appeared. By rights each later one should surpass those before it, should it not? Yet history has proven that Master Kumārajīva's translation has the greatest power to take hold of beings, that is, it best accords with the meaning of the sūtra, and has been widely circulated without decline.

The Buddha said: Excellent! Excellent! Subhuti, just as you have said, the Tathāgata truly protects and cares for all bodhisattvas and perfectly entrusts and instructs all bodhisattvas. Now listen with all attention, and I shall tell you. Good men and good women who have awakened the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should thus abide and thus subdue their minds.

The Buddha said: How wonderful! How wonderful! Subhuti, just as you have said, this is truly the Tathāgata's best protection and care for all bodhisattvas and his best education and guidance for all bodhisattvas! Listen with all attention, and I shall expound separately for you this method of abiding in the path and subduing the mind. Good men and good women who have awakened the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should thus sustain their dwelling and thus subdue their minds.

【How wonderful】How wonderful! A word of praise. 【Listen with all attention】To listen with all attention. 【Thus】In this way. Here the two words “thus” (rúshì) point vaguely to the following text—“should thus abide” refers to Division Four, and “thus subdue their minds” refers to Division Three.

The Buddha spoke two “Excellent!” in succession to praise Subhuti. The first “Excellent!” praises Subhuti for being able to understand the Buddha's manifestation. The Buddha confirmed that Subhuti understood without error, saying: Subhuti, as you have said, I manifest thus day after day—this is truly the Tathāgata's best protection and care for all bodhisattvas and his best education and guidance for all bodhisattvas! The second “Excellent!” praises Subhuti's wisdom and compassionate mind in being able to request the solution of two questions that vex practitioners to no end and urgently require resolution—how should one sustain one's dwelling? How should one subdue the mind?

Next, with regard to the two questions Subhuti had requested, the Buddha said: The two questions you have raised—listen to them with all attention, and I shall explain them in detail for you. Good men and good women who have awakened the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should thus sustain their dwelling and should thus subdue their minds.
So be it, World-Honored One! We wish with joy to hear.
Subhuti respectfully replied: Yes, World-Honored One! I very much long for, and joyfully wish to hear, your exposition on these two questions.
The Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra (the Flower Ornament Scripture)

Volume Thirty-Four” says: “As the thirsty long for cool water, as the hungry yearn for fine food, as the sick recall good medicine, as the bee craves sweet honey; so are we also, wishing to hear the Dharma of sweet dew!”

【So be it】“Wéi” is a word of assent. For example, the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says: “At that time, the Buddha told the Mahāsattva Bodhisattva Mahāmati: I shall now explain to you the characteristics of the difference of the mind-made body. Listen! Listen! Think well upon it. Mahāmati said: Yes (wéi).” “Rán” means earnestly wishing to listen to the World-Honored One's detailed exposition of the two “thus” phrases. 【So be it, World-Honored One!】Subhuti respectfully replied, expressing deep willingness. 【We wish with joy to hear】To joyfully desire to hear the Dharma.

Good men and good women who have awakened the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should thus abide and thus subdue their minds”—this passage has historically had two other interpretations; in order better to understand the meaning of the sūtra, let us examine them as follows:
First: the World-Honored One's two “thus” phrases already answered Subhuti's two questions—“How should they abide? How should they subdue their minds?”—only that Subhuti did not understand.

This reading is not sound, because even if Subhuti did not understand the two “thus” phrases, he would not fail to grasp the World-Honored One's tone. If the World-Honored One's two “thus” phrases were in fact answering Subhuti's two “how” questions, yet the Venerable One did not understand, he would have said something like “I beg the World-Honored One, in his great compassion and pity, to expound them separately for the sake of beings,” rather than joyfully falling in with the World-Honored One's tone and saying “So be it, World-Honored One! We wish with joy to hear.” This may be compared to the passage in the Lotus Sūtra

“Chapter of Skillful Means, Division Two”: “At that time, the Buddha told Śāriputra: ... Now hear attentively, and I shall tell you. Śāriputra replied: So be it, World-Honored One! We wish with joy to hear.”

Second: the World-Honored One's two “thus” phrases already answered Subhuti's two questions—“How should they abide? How should they subdue their minds?”—and although Subhuti understood, the great assembly had not yet understood, so on its behalf he begged the World-Honored One to explain in full.

This reading is also unsound. At the very beginning of “Division Fourteen: The Extinction of Marks and the Stillness of Thoughts” it says: “At that time, when Subhuti heard this sūtra, he understood deeply its purport and meaning, and his tears fell as he wept, and he addressed the Buddha, saying: How rare, O World-Honored One! The Buddha has spoken such a profound and deep sūtra; since the beginning of the past I have obtained the wisdom-eye, yet I have never heard such a sūtra.” From this passage we see that Subhuti had not understood before this point.

In fact, the questions Subhuti asked—“How should they abide? How should they subdue their minds?”—were questions of a profound depth. Subhuti was already an arhat, his erroneous views and afflictions already cut off, and he was foremost in comprehending emptiness; the superficial “How should they abide? How should they subdue their minds?” he not only knew thoroughly but had long since put into practice. The present questions were raised in response to what he awakened to, from the World-Honored One's everyday activities such as donning the robe and taking up the bowl, to the World-Honored One's profound intention and ultimate practice. Subhuti's question at last brought forth the Diamond Sūtra, of which it is said “all the Buddhas, and the Dharma of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all the Buddhas, come forth from this sūtra”!

Therefore the meaning of “Now listen with all attention, and I shall tell you. Good men and good women who have awakened the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should thus abide and thus subdue their minds” is: Listen with all attention, and I shall explain in detail for you the two questions you have raised. Good men and good women who have awakened the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should thus sustain their dwelling and should thus subdue their minds.

This is like a person asking about a complicated problem, and the answerer says, “It is thus.” This is a vocative opening phrase, used at the head of a discourse to draw the listener's attention. Its meaning is: In what follows I will explain this problem to you in detail. It does not mean that the phrase “It is thus” already answers the question.

For this passage, Master Xuanzang's translation is: “At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Subhuti (Shànxiàn), saying: Excellent! Excellent! Subhuti, so it is, so it is. As you have said, even to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Fully Enlightened One, who is able to take under his supreme protection all bodhisattva mahāsattvas, even to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Fully Enlightened One, who is able, with his supreme entrusting, to entrust all bodhisattva mahāsattvas. Therefore, Subhuti! You should listen with all attention, and be excellently mindful,
I shall explain for you, distinguishing and expounding

—all those who are intent on the bodhisattva vehicle should thus abide, thus practice, and thus subdue their minds. The Venerable Subhuti addressed the Buddha, saying: So it is, so it is. World-Honored One! We wish with joy to hear.”
Please pay special attention to the eight characters “I shall explain for you, distinguishing and expounding.”
【Venerable】A common designation of a bhikshu, because a bhikshu not only possesses the life-span of the world but also possesses the wisdom-life of the Dharma-body.

Therefore Subhuti's reply—“So be it, World-Honored One! We wish with joy to hear”—means: Yes, World-Honored One! I very much long for, and joyfully wish to hear, your full exposition of these two questions. Hence it is that in Division Fourteen we have “Subhuti, hearing this sūtra, understood deeply its purport and meaning, and his tears fell as he wept, and he addressed the Buddha, saying: How rare, O World-Honored One! The Buddha has spoken such a profound and deep sūtra; since the beginning of the past I have obtained the wisdom-eye, yet I have never heard such a sūtra.”—it is precisely this!
The unsurpassed, profound, and subtle Dharma, encountered only after a hundred thousand myriads of eons;

In this division, Subhuti raised two extremely important questions: How should they abide? How should they subdue their minds? These form the theme that runs throughout the whole text. In order to facilitate understanding of the passages below, let us now first set out the answers.
Question: How should one abide?
